items.text: Double-click a window's title bar to zoom it. Double-click again and it returns to its old size.
Drag a window against the left or right edge of the screen and it fills that half. Drag it away to set it free again.
Rest the pointer on a window's zoom button for a moment: a small menu offers left half, right half, full size and both side by side.
Right-click a window's title bar for its layout options — minimise, zoom, left or right half.
The desktop remembers your windows. Close the tab, come back tomorrow, and everything is where you left it.
Right-click an app in the Dock and choose “Keep in Dock” — or drag your favourites into the order you like.
Deleted notes and tasks wait in the trash for 30 days. Changed your mind? Put them back.
Drop a text file onto the desktop and it opens in the editor. A picture opens in the image viewer.
Every wallpaper motif is drawn by your browser — nothing to download, sharp on every screen.
Light or dark, blue or green: Settings → Appearance changes the mode and the accent colour.
The best time for a backup was yesterday. The second best is now: Settings → Data → Backup saves notes, tasks and preferences in one file.
On a phone the desktop folds into one window at a time — the same apps, made for your thumb.
Ctrl+K — or ⌘K on keyboards that have it — opens the search: apps, bookmarks, pages and more.
F3 shows all open windows side by side. Pick one with the arrow keys and press Enter.
Ctrl and the key to the left of 1 switch to the next window. Add Shift to go the other way.
In the menu bar the arrow keys move between the menus and through their entries. No mouse needed.
Esc closes an open menu and puts the focus back where it came from.
In the editor, Alt+Z turns word wrap on and off.
Here, Space or N shows the next fortune and the left arrow goes back — twenty steps at most.
Ctrl+C without a text selection copies the fortune you are reading. The calculator does the same with its result.
Shift+F10 or the context menu key opens the context menu of whatever has the focus.
Not a single node of this desktop is built with innerHTML. That is why a strict Content Security Policy costs it nothing.
Native ES modules need no bundler: the browser loads exactly the files a page imports, and nothing else.
Logical CSS properties such as margin-inline-start make a layout work in right-to-left languages — without a second stylesheet.
Plurals are not “add an s”. Intl.PluralRules knows that some languages have three, four or six forms.
A version in the file name plus Cache-Control: immutable — and returning visitors never download a file twice.
A JSON Feed is just JSON. If you can write an object, you can publish a feed — this desktop reads one for its notifications.
Static files on a good web server are hard to beat: fast, cheap, and nothing to patch at three in the morning.
Treat everything you read back from storage as a stranger. Today's bug report often starts with yesterday's data.
Want another language? Copy the locales/en folder, translate the texts, add the code to the configuration. That is all.
Every button here that shows only an icon has a name for screen readers. A tooltip alone is not a label.
Colour never carries a message on its own: an error also gets words.
Normal text needs a contrast of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background. Try a pair of colours in the contrast checker.
Headings are the table of contents for people who listen to a page. Use them in order.
prefers-reduced-motion is a request, not a suggestion. This desktop skips its animations when you ask for it.
Focus should never get lost: when a window closes, it moves to the next one.
“Click here” tells nobody where a link goes. Good link texts make sense on their own.
This fortune cookie has no calories and leaves no crumbs in your keyboard.
The trash empties itself after 30 days. If only the inbox would do the same.
Why did the developer keep the calculator in the Dock? Because in the end, everything has to add up.
Lorem ipsum is not a language. We checked — it is not in the locales folder either.
A window walks into a Dock. The Dock asks: why so minimised today?
There is no cloud. There is only someone else's computer — and this one, right here in your browser.
